properties.field_incident_overview:
On May 14, 2026 a powerful storm system moved through southwest Kansas. Lightning strikes, fueled by strong winds and very dry vegetation, started multiple fires across the landscape. The fires quickly surpassed the local and mutual aid response. State assistance was requested. Aviation, KFS DFMOs, and in-state Wildfire Taskforces were mobilized. Many of the initial fires merged and are now being managed as a complex fire. Kansas Governor Kelly issued a State of Emergency Declaration on Friday, May 15, 2026. Local declarations have been issued; there is no federal emergency declaration. 

On Monday, May 18, the Meade County Fires are now under one Incident Command System and will be called the Meade Lake Complex. 

On May 20, 2026, the fire region received precipitation and higher humidity, which helped increase containment on both complexes. Non-local resources will be returned to their home units, and the fires will be monitored and patrolled by the local fire departments. The weather conditions in southwest Kansas have not dramatically changed. There is still potential for new starts to burn intensely and grow rapidly. 

The fires under the Meade Lake Complex are the Wolf Canyon Fire, the Meade County Complex 1 and 2, the Proffitt Lake fire, and the 2 unstaffed fires in the southern part of the county.  

Meade Lake Complex -  Jeff Latham and Troy Mueller - Incident Commanders      

  • 91,616 acres
  • 100% contained

The 500-Acre Pond Fire and the Herman Range Fire grew together on Sunday May, 17, 2026. All fires in Clark County will also be a complex of fires. The complex will include the Bouziden Range Fire and the Lexington Fire

Herman Range Complex - Chad Maybery Incident Commander

properties.field_incident_overview:
The South Fork Fire ignited on June 9, 2026, in the Soldier Creek Wilderness area of the Nebraska National Forest’s Pine Ridge Ranger District near Crawford, Nebraska. Local responders, U.S. Forest Service crews and volunteer firefighting partners engaged the fire early as dry fuels, steep terrain and strong winds drove rapid spread. U.S. Highway 20 was closed by the Nebraska Department of Transportation as the fire jumped the highway. A red flag warning was in effect through Wednesday, June 10.

By June 10, the fire had grown to nearly 9,000 acres and Nebraska’s Governor Pillen officially issued an emergency declaration for the South Fork Fire. It was fueled by rugged terrain, dry vegetation including timber and grassy undergrowth, and strong winds. On June 11 at 6 am the Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2, under the command of Jay Mickey, assumed control of the fire.

On June 12, containment increased to 7% even as the fire grew to about 28,067 acres. Resources including National Guard units, ground crews, dozers and aircraft focused on defending the towns of Crawford and the Fort Robinson State Park area. The Red Cross established community shelter options at the Chadron State College–Andrews Hall.

By June 15, containment was at 55% and the fire had grown to 38,914 acres. 581 personnel were supporting the fire. Forecasters predicted that the week ahead would bring sustained winds anticipated between 23 and 30 miles per hour, and the possibility of gusts escalating to as high as 50 miles per hour. 

Nebraska’s Governor, Jim Pillen received an operational visit of the South Fork Fire on June 16. He visited ICP and was provided with a comprehensive briefing. He had the opportunity to communicate with members of his constituency as well as incident team members. 

Containment reached 80% on June 17, with the acres climbing to 39,057. Although conditions continued to change, fire activity was generally quiet. A NIROPS flight (a thermal imaging aircraft used to map active wildfires) was ordered after several areas of hot spots were discovered. 

Line is now in place around the entire fire perimeter. Crews are working to secure and mop up the containment line and will continue for several days. Suppression repair work is also u begin underway and will continue in the next few days. 

On June 20th the overall acreage of the South Fork Fire increased to 39,696 due to more accurate satellite mapping showing previously unseen grassy areas and containment increased to 90%.

Rocky Mountain CIMT2 transfered command to the Nebraska Type 3 team on Sunday, June 21, 2026, at 6 p.m.  

Please follow the Nebraska National Forest on Facebook and the Nebraska National Forest website's Alerts and Notices page for further updates.

During the current operational period, fire activity remained minimal, consisting primarily of smoldering and creeping within the interior. Firefighters will continue mop up operations and perimeter patrols to secure containment lines and keep the fire within the established perimeter. Fuels consist primarily of medium logging slash, brush, and tall grasses.

A Red Flag Warning remains in effect through Sunday evening, with dry breezy conditions and near-critical fire weather expected to continue into next week. Gusty winds may produce interior flare ups and localized spotting potential over the next 72 hours; however, no current threat to communities, infrastructure, or other values at risk has been identified.

There has been no reported damage to structures or infrastructure, no civilian impacts. Approximately 192 personnel remain assigned to the incident in support of suppression and containment efforts.

Operational priorities remained focused on patrolling and securing the fire perimeter, completing mop-up where needed, implementing suppression repair, and maintaining containment.

The fire is approximately six miles from the Hoh Rain Forest administrative site. The Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, campground, and trails all remain open to the public.

Firefighters are using indirect confinement tactics as part of a full-suppression strategy. These tactics include removing vegetation around recreation and administrative infrastructure and using helicopters to drop water to cool host spots and keep the fire within its current footprint. The fire is constrained by natural features on a couple flanks, where fire managers have determined it is 27% contained.

High relative humidity and periodic precipitation may constrain fire behavior, but are unlikely to extinguish the fire.

Smoke: Smoke may be visible from various locations on the Olympic Peninsula. Air quality can change quickly.  For current smoke information, visit: https://fire.airnow.gov

Fire Restrictions: Olympic National Park implemented fire restrictions June 25th. Dispersed and backcountry fires are prohibited. Fires within established metal fire rings in developed campgrounds and picnic areas are exempt from this prohibition. Propane and gas stoves are allowed, if operated at least three feet away from flammable vegetation and forest litter.

The fire burned in mixed fuel types and steep terrain. The fire grew very quickly in the first 24 hours, prompting evacuations of nearby communities and a closure order on Fishlake National Forest.

In the first days of the incident, cooler temperatures allowed firefighters to actively engage the fire, installing containment and contingency lines before increased temperatures and heavier winds created critical fire weather conditions. 

Fuels are exceptionally dry for this time of year and contributed to extreme fire behavior, but the lines created in the first week of GBT7's tenure have held and largely curtailed fire spread. Since July 3, fire behavior has remained moderate. On July 10, all evacuation orders were lifted and the Fishlake National Forest Closure was reduced in size to reopen popular recreation areas to the south of the fire.

The Gold Mountain Fire was discovered on June 27, 2026, at approximately 5:33 pm 2 miles northeast of Ouray, CO. Fire initially started burning in mixed conifer vegetation located on inaccessible terrain above the east side of Highway 550. Local, State, and Federal initial attack fire resources were ordered immediately. The fire spread quickly running up steep slopes. A local Type 3 Incident Management Team was assigned on June 27, 2026. Aviation resources were ordered throughout the next day, but high winds and terrain features shut down the use of aviation resources. Fire became very active, with group torching and crowning, increasing the fire growth to the east by 2,000 acres. Fire resources provided public safety and worked to protect structures. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 3 was ordered on June 28, 2026, and took command on June 29, 2026, at 6 pm.  Red Flag conditions over the following week led to extreme fire behavior increasing the fire growth to over 30,000 acres by July 6, 2026. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 2 assumed command July 14, 2026 following a coordinated, planned transition. Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 1 assumed command July 26, 2026 following a coordinated, planned transition. 

Firefighters are using a risk-based suppression strategy that prioritizes public and firefighter safety while protecting communities, critical infrastructure, water systems and access along the Highway 550 corridor. Crews continue to mop up and strengthen fire lines near Highway 550 and Cow Creek, secure the fire edge around Nate Creek, and construct and reinforce indirect line along the western perimeter toward Bureau of Land Management lands and south toward Silver Jack Reservoir. 

Where direct engagement is unsafe or impractical, firefighters are using natural features, indirect containment lines, point protection around homes and other values at risk, and pumps, hoses and large water tanks to support structure protection. Aerial resources continue to monitor and support operations along inaccessible portions of the fire. Although thunderstorms may bring periods of rain, critically dry fuels, lightning and erratic outflow winds remain concerns.

Background: On the afternoon of Sunday, June 21, the Mogollon Baldy lookout detected a lightning-caused fire on Sacaton Mountain (elevation 10,658 feet) in the Gila Wilderness. The fire, which is on the Glenwood Ranger District, was initially about 4.5 miles west of the lookout tower. 

Firefighters quickly conducted an aerial assessment and estimated the fire—burning in brush, timber, logs, and snags—was about 2 acres and exhibiting moderate fire behavior. By late evening, the lookout reported the fire had grown to approximately 4 acres.

The fire’s location presents extreme risks to both ground and aerial firefighters: It is burning among numerous snags, a dense tangle of fallen trees, and thick brush regeneration from the 2012 Whitewater-Baldy Fire. The landscape is very rugged and steep (e.g., 40–60 percent slopes). Safety zones and escape routes are nonexistent. Emergency extraction times would be unacceptably long (i.e., 6+ hours) and logistically difficult. High-elevation flying, especially during hot weather, is very hazardous and an unacceptable transfer of risk to the pilot.

Links - Daily Update (pdf)     |     Daily Informational Map (pdf)     |     Fire Progression Map    |     Daily Operations Update (video) 

 

The Biscar Fire started from a lightning strike on July 18, 2026 within Lassen County.  It grew quickly with warm temperatures and strong winds pushing it eastward across Highway 395.  It is currently mapped at 69,352 acres with 97% containment.

Fire Activity: Fire activity has been minimal despite elevated fire weather conditions. Containment lines around the fire continue to be reinforced. Crews have been checking integrity of the containment lines using a tactic called “cold trailing,” where fire fighters walk along these lines to verify that no heat persists. 

About 200 firefighters were released Sunday, and additional 200 were released Monday and made available to other fires in the region.  Resources continue to be made available for reassignments today as they finish their tasks on the Biscar Fire.  A National Preparedness Level 5 (Highest Level) indicates a significant amount of fire activity nationally with resources (crews, engines, aircraft) mostly being committed; and therefore fewer resources available to respond to new ignitions.

California Interagency Incident Management Team 3 has demobilized from the Biscar Fire today, and will be reassigned to the Castle Fire in southern Oregon.  The Team thanks the residents and Emergency Management staff of Lassen County, CA and Washoe County, NV for their support and dedication during the Biscar Fire.

Why the strange name?  Fires are often named after geographic features near the fire, and in this case, Biscar Reservoir is located just a few miles south of where the fire was first reported.  Pierre “Pete” Biscar (1881–1947),  was a French-born rancher who settled in Secret Valley, California, and constructed the first reservoir at the mouth of Snowstorm Canyon.

Incident Objectives:

  • Provide safety for first responders and the public through risk analysis and hazard mitigation.
  • Minimize acres burned utilizing direct extinguishment tactics.
  • Utilize resources where they can be most successful and ensure tactics have a high probability of success.
  • Protect and minimize impacts to communities, private property, infrastructure, cultural, natural resources and Sage Grouse habitat.
  • Strengthen collaboration and relationships with cooperators, ranchers, tribal communities, and the public by delivering accurate information while seeking opportunities to build new relationships.

Evacuation Orders: 

California  

  • Evacuation Orders: All Evacuation Orders have been lifted.  
  • Evacuation Warnings: Zone LAS-553 remains in an evacuation warning.  
  • All other zones have been placed back into a normal status.  
  • Conditions may change rapidly due to changing conditions on this fire, or a new fire.  Be prepared to leave at a moment's notice.
  • Interactive Evacuation Map is available through https://protect.genasys.com/ 

For shelter information call (530) 254-4500: or visit the Lassen County Sheriff's Office Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/LassenSheriff/ 

Nevada

  • Level 2 (Set), and Level 3 (Go Now) Evacuation recommendations have been issued for portions of central Washoe County.  
  • Interactive Evacuation Map is available through https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/46cb79ef933d4485b9966a9730e2d944/page/Perimeter/ 

Please note that California and Nevada use different, though similar, programs.  Evacuation status information for each state is displayed within their respective programs.  

Area Closures: The Bureau of Land Management has instituted a temporary closure of public lands for the Biscar Fire.  Public lands near Snowstorm Road and Vincent Canyon, northeast of Susanville in Lassen County, are closed for wildland fire fighting operations.  Pursuant to 43 CFR 8364.1, this temporary closure is being implemented for public and firefighter safety during emergency fire suppression actions.  View the Full Closure Order and Map.

Fire Restrictions: The Bureau of Land Management issued seasonal fire restrictions effective July 15th for BLM-managed public lands within Lassen, Modoc, Plumas, Sierra, Siskiyou and Shasta counties in California and Washoe County, Nevada. These seasonal restrictions are in addition to the year-round, statewide fire prevention order. These fire orders for Applegate and Eagle Lake field offices are in place to help prevent wildfires and will remain in effect until further notice.

The fire restrictions prohibit campfires and barbecues except within established campfire rings and barbecue grills in certain designated recreation sites:   Read more at https://www.blm.gov/announcement/blm-announces-seasonal-fire-restrictions-ne-california-nw-nevada-0 

Highway Closures: Highway 395 has reopened with no traffic restrictions.       Please use caution when traveling in the area as firefighters may be working near the roads, and anticipate an increased amount of heavy equipment between the fire area and Susanville.  https://roads.dot.ca.gov/?roadnumber=395 

Smoke Impacts:  Very little smoke is being produced by the Biscar Fire.  Please visit https://fire.airnow.gov/?lang=en#7.34/40.599/-119.644 for smoke information from the Biscar Fire.    Fore information about the impacts of smoke, and ways to protect your health, please visit https://www.airnow.gov/air-quality-and-health/fires-and-your-health/ 

About the Bureau of Land Management - Northern California District.  The BLM’s Northern California District manages about 3.5 million acres of public lands, covering a diverse landscape, ranging from the arid and rugged Great Basin to the fog shrouded forests of the North Coast. The Redding-based district office oversees field offices in Alturas, Arcata, Redding and Susanville and a field station in Cedarville. The district contains two distinct regions. On the east, the Applegate and Eagle Lake field offices oversee vast expanses of public lands in a high desert landscape, including about a million and a half acres in far western Nevada. Small communities depend on public lands for economic benefits, primarily through livestock grazing, and tourism uses ranging from hunting to mountain biking. These lands provide habitat for 14 wild horse herds and special status species, such as greater sage grouse. On the west, the Arcata and Redding field offices manage smaller, scattered blocks of public land with more emphasis on recreation demands from urban areas.

The Castle Fire was first reported on July 22, 2026.  It is currently estimated to be 3,612 acres and 67% contained.  

Today we say farewell and give thanks to California Incident Management Team 3 who are demobilizing and welcome FDNY Incident Management Team to the Castle fire.  FDNY will manage the Castle Fire with the assistance of an integrated International CIMT from Australia.  California Complex Incident Management Team 3 has left for home and a couple of well deserved days off after 14 days of work between the Biscar Fire and the Castle Fire.

Nick McCarthy with the Australian Incident Command Team talks about the role of Fire Behavior Analysist and the new and unique challenges of modelling fire behavior in Oregon.   https://www.facebook.com/reel/1072162712427661 

Fire Activity: Firefighters continue to patrol and mop up during the day and prepare for firing operations overnight if the conditions allow. Increased fire behavior is being observed within the fire perimeter due to the hot and dry weather conditions but well within containment lines. All lines were held during the day with no spots detected. The spot fire from a few days ago, continues to be two acres with a fire line and hose surrounding it. The fire is being managed for full suppression. 

Fire Weather: The thermal trough is now moving east followed by a strong upper ridge, creating possible unstable conditions. Above average dry and high temperatures with critically low humidity in the afternoons continue, resulting in a heightened risk of fire activity. The Forest Fire Danger remains Very High.

Incident Objectives:  

  • Provide safety for first responders and the public through robust risk analysis and hazard mitigation.
  • Minimize acres burned and utilize resources where they can be most successful and ensure tactics have the highest probability of success.
  • Protect and minimize impacts to communities, private property, infrastructure, cultural and natural resources.
  • Strengthen collaboration and relationships with international partners, cooperators, timber industry, tribal communities, and the public by delivering timely, accurate information while seeking opportunities to build new relationships.

Forest Closures: Umpqua National Forest has expanded the closure area in order to protect the public and provide a safe environment for firefighters. The expanded closure order #06-15-02-26-02 supersedes closure order #06-15-02-26-01. 

All National Forest System lands, roads and trails will be closed to public within the closure area. The closure will remain in effect until conditions allow for reopening.  Visit the Umpqua Alerts and Notices page at  https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/umpqua/alerts/castle-fire-closure - You may also click on the Closure Order (pdf) and Closure Order Map (pdf). 

Public Use Restrictions:  As of Friday, July 24, 2026 the Umpqua National Forest moved to Public Use Restrictions (PURs) Stage 2 across the whole Forest. In PURs Stage 2, campfires in wilderness and public firewood cutting (with an internal combustion engine) will no longer be allowed. Campfires within Forest Service-constructed concrete or metal fire rings within designated developed recreation sites are exempt.  More Information is available at https://www.fs.usda.gov/r06/umpqua/alerts/public-use-restrictions-stage-2 

Smoke Impacts: With a significant number of fires burning within Oregon, please take steps to protect yourself from smoke.  Smoke can irritate the eyes and lungs and worsen some medical conditions. People most at risk include infants and young children, people with heart or lung disease, older adults and pregnant people.  Smoke levels can change rapidly depending on weather. Check current conditions on the U.S. Interagency Wildland Fire Air Quality Response Program, the Oregon Smoke Information Blog, DEQ’s Air Quality Index, or by downloading the free OregonAIR app on your smartphone.

About the Forest: The Umpqua National Forest protects 982,510 acres of forest across Douglas, Lane, and Jackson Counties. High Cascades glaciation, whitewater rapids, and explosive volcanic events have shaped the Forest's spectacular scenery and abundant natural resources. Verdant stands of hemlock, fir and cedar transition to forests of mixed conifers and hardwoods at lower elevations, while alpine ecosystems dominate high peaks like Mount Thielsen. The Forest's waterways and diverse ecosystems create desirable habitat for many species of fish and wildlife, in addition to providing outstanding recreational opportunities to our local communities and visitors.

The Forest is headquartered in Roseburg and has four ranger districts: Cottage Grove, Diamond Lake, North Umpqua, and Tiller. The Forest is also the home of the Dorena Genetic Research Center and Wolf Creek Job Corps Center. The Dorena Center, located in Cottage Grove, houses breeding programs for disease-resistant trees, a native plant development program, and the National Tree Climbing Program. The Wolf Creek Job Corps in Glide is a federal tuition-free training and education program.

properties.field_incident_description:
The Big Grass Fire started on July 23, 2026, following a lightning strike. Fuels in the area consist of brush, short grasses, and tall grasses. The fire will continue to exhibit extreme fire behavior, with rapid rates of spread in all directions when smoke lifts and winds pick up in the afternoon.

The fire has advanced to the point where protection of the wildland-urban interface has become the primary operational focus. Point protection operations are underway for multiple residences as the fire continues to progress. Continued fire spread is expected into Idaho along both the northern and southern portions of the fire area, with steady eastward progression up South Mountain.

Numerous residential structures, outbuildings, and associated improvements remain threatened as the fire continues to advance toward the community of Jordan Valley. Additional values at risk include the Wild and Scenic River corridor, North Fork Campground, Three Forks Campground, priority sage-grouse habitat, essential pronghorn habitat, grazing allotments, a Remote Automated Weather Station (RAWS), the South Mountain communication site, and numerous mining operations farther north. Continued fire spread has the potential to impact residential properties, critical infrastructure, recreational facilities, wildlife habitat, rangeland resources, and fire weather monitoring capabilities.
properties.field_incident_overview:
An aggressive full-suppression strategy is in place for the Big Grass Fire to protect communities, structures, critical infrastructure, and other valuable resources at risk. Efforts are focused on minimizing impacts on public, private, and state lands, as well as natural and cultural resources. This is being done in coordination with the local Rangeland Fire Protection Association (RFPA) and cooperating agencies. 

Current Situation: Yesterday, most of the fire activity was on the southeast perimeter. The fire made a significant run east towards Deep Creek. Crews continued to make significant progress constructing a containment line along the fire’s edge in the Boulder Creek area, working southeast towards Josephine Road. Additionally, firefighters continued to work along the Mud Flat Road, keeping the active fire to the north.   

Today, given the combination of hot and dry conditions and gusty afternoon winds, fire activity will increase. The priority remains on completing the containment line from Boulder Creek to Josephine Road and continuing to hold the fire north of the Mud Flat Road. Crews are also working to secure fire lines around ranches, private properties, and critical infrastructure in the South Mountain area. Further south, crews will be evaluating suppression strategies for the fire moving towards Deep Creek. The rest of the fire is in patrol status, and firefighters will be monitoring those areas. 

New Evacuation:  Last night, the Owyhee County Sheriff expanded a Level 3 GO to Antelope Ridge Road south to Big Springs Ranch Road, south to the Owyhee River Canyon to include Dickshooter, west to the Oregon Stateline to include the 45 Ranch.  

Level 3 GO evacuation order is also in place for Triangle Reservoir, Pleasant Valley, South Mountain, Pleasant Valley Road to the City of Triangle, City of Triangle to the Triangle Reservoir, Flint Creek Road, Juniper Mountain Road, and the west portion of Mud Flat Road. A Level 2 SET status has been issued for Silver City.  

BLM Area Closure: The Bureau of Land Management Owyhee Field Office has issued a temporary closure of the entire area. The entire area south of Trout Creek Road and Silver City Road to the East Fork and Main Stem of the Owyhee River and from the Oregon border east to Highway 78 and Highway 51 is temporarily closed. For more information on BLM area closures and maps, visit: BLM Idaho Closures and  BLM Oregon Closures.  

Weather and Air Quality: High pressure over the desert Southwest continues to bring very hot and dry conditions to the area through the upcoming weekend. Today will be the hottest day with afternoon high temperatures in the 90s to low 100s. Relative humidity will drop into the single digits, with poor overnight recovery. Southwest to west winds, gusting around 20 to 25 MPH, can be expected this afternoon.  Degraded air quality will persist over the area. For more information on Air Quality at your location, visit www.airnow.gov for real-time data. 

Cooperating Agencies: Jordan Valley RFPA, Owyhee RFPA, Malheur County Sheriff’s Office, Owyhee County Sheriff’s Office, Owyhee County OEM, Idaho OEM, ODT, Idaho Power, Idaho Department of Lands.

The fire reached 689 acres and is currently at 100 percent containment. Firefighters were able to establish constructive containment lines, and the fire is holding within the current fire perimeter. The cause of the fire is still under investigation.

 

The fire is approximately 50 acres and is located on East Grade Road near Lake Henshaw and Highway 76. The cause of the fire is under investigation and there is no containment.  There is one structure threatened and a full road closure on East Grade Road.

The Grade Fire is burning in medium fuels and brush vegetation with moderate fire behavior.  The fire is burning in a north by northeast direction. 

There are currently 9 engines, two hand crews, two water tenders, 4 air tankers, and two helicopters responding to the incident, with more resources being ordered.

The Bare Fire is located north of Bare Pass and east of Bare Creek on the Big Piney Ranger District of the Bridger-Teton National Forest. The fire is burning in heavy timber fuels and is exhibiting increased fire activity, including torching and spotting, as fuel moisture decreases and temperatures rise in the afternoon. The fire has crossed jurisdictional boundaries, including Bureau of Land Management land and private land in Sublette County, adjacent to the Forest boundary. Cause of the fire is undetermined.

Wyoming Team 3, a Type 3 Incident Management Team, took command of the fire from local resources at 6:00 a.m. on Thursday, August 6.

Fire managers are implementing direct extinguishment and indirect confinement strategies on the Bare Fire. A direct extinguishment strategy is when firefighters engage the active flame front directly to stop fire spread. An indirect confinement strategy is when firefighters work away from the active flame front to steer or contain the fire.

properties.field_incident_overview:
The Double Springs Fire is a lightning-caused wildfire burning approximately 21 miles southeast of Challis, Idaho, in the Christian Gulch area of the Salmon-Challis National Forest. The fire was detected on July 24, 2026, and is burning in steep, rugged terrain with heavy timber, dead and down fuels, and limited road access.

Since the fire was discovered, firefighters have implemented a full suppression strategy focused on protecting firefighter and public safety while minimizing fire growth. Due to the steep slopes, loose shale, and challenging terrain, suppression efforts have relied on a combination of existing road systems, natural barriers, and strategically constructed containment lines rather than direct attack in some portions of the fire.

Throughout the incident, weather conditions have played a significant role in fire behavior. Periods of hot temperatures, low relative humidity, and gusty winds have resulted in increased fire activity, while cooler temperatures, higher humidity, and overnight inversions have moderated fire behavior and allowed crews to strengthen containment lines and improve access into the fire area.

As the incident has evolved, additional firefighting resources have been assigned, and the fire transitioned to a Type 3 Incident Management Organization to support ongoing suppression operations.
